Let $b$ be the bit length of $n$, $K$ the address-chunk width in bits, $\ell$ the address bits of the longest axis, and $p$ the precision, setting the $2^{-p}$ grid of the [Fixed-point Gaussian dyadic records](fixed-point.md).

derivations.quote: The layer conditions hold with room to spare: $\tau(1+c/\beta)<1-31\cdot2^{-55}<\lambda$, since $\tau(1+c/\beta)=1-31\cdot2^{-55}-2^{-105}$ and $\lambda=1-8\cdot2^{-55}$.
Take the power of two $T$ in $[4n/b,8n/b)$, so $Tp\in[24n,48n)$.

Let $r=2^{\lceil(\log_2T)/d\rceil}$ and $\ell=\log_2r$; choose $d\ell-\log_2T\in[0,d)$ of the axis lengths to be $r/2$ and the others $r$, with the last axis of length $r$. This is possible as $0\le d\ell-\log_2T<d$, and the product is $2^{d\ell-(d\ell-\log_2T)}=T$.

These choices give $Tp=\Theta(n)$, $d=\Theta(p^\epsilon)$, $K=\Theta(p^{\epsilon c})$, $\ell=\Theta(p^{1-\epsilon})$, $r=2^{\Theta(p^{1-\epsilon})}$, so the comparison constants $a_d=a_r=1/12$, $b_d=1$, $b_r=1/3$, $C_\ell=1$ can be fixed for all lengths at once: $b/2\le\log_2T\le b$ gives $\tfrac1{12}p^\epsilon\le d\le p^\epsilon$ and $\tfrac p{12d}\le\ell\le\tfrac p{3d}$.
As $\lceil A\rceil\le2A$ and $8\sqrt{12}<28$, $\gamma<28d^2\sqrt b\le28b^{1/2+2\epsilon}\le28b^{2/3}$ follows, so $2\le\alpha<\sqrt p$ eventually and $\gamma=o(b)$.

By the prime-interval lemma, for $0<\eta<1/4$ and $x>e^{2/\eta}$ the interval $(1-2\eta)x<q\le(1-\eta)x$ contains at least $\eta x/(2\log x)$ primes; both $x=r/2$ and $x=r$ qualify since $\log x>8d=2/\eta$, and the count $x/(8d\log x)$ exceeds $d$.
The two intervals are disjoint and each holds more than $d$ primes, so choose distinct odd primes with $(1-2\eta)t_i<s_i\le(1-\eta)t_i$; $\gcd(s_i,t_i)=1$ as $t_i$ is a power of two.
Multiplying the lower bounds and applying strict Bernoulli gives $S/T>(1-1/(2d))^d>1/2$ for $d\ge2$.
With $\theta_i=t_i/s_i-1\ge\eta/(1-\eta)>\eta$ we get $\alpha^4\theta_i>12d^2b/(4d)=3db\ge6b=p$, the separation hypothesis of the resampling lemma; also $t_i\le r\le T<2^p$.

The deterministic search for the primes takes $n^{o(1)}=o(n)$ time, since its logarithm is $o(p)$ and $p=\Theta(\log n)$; all primes and length parameters are generated by the machine, not given as advice.
